eschew

/es-CHOO/ - rhymes with too · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Eschew means to deliberately avoid a thing, habit, or practice on principle.

The columnist eschews exclamation points, arguing that a sentence should earn its emphasis.

Example

Their grandmother eschews the elevator, taking the four flights to her apartment at her own steady pace, rain or shine.

Eschew is more pointed than avoid because it names a standing, deliberate policy — she is not afraid of the elevator and does not merely miss it now and then; she has ruled it out, on principle, every time.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

forgo: To forgo is to do without something pleasant or advantageous, often just this once — you forgo dessert, a bonus, a day off. Eschew is sterner and standing: a settled policy of avoiding a practice on principle, every time, not a single sacrifice made in passing.

spurn: To spurn is to reject something offered — an invitation, an advance, a deal — with open scorn, in the moment. Eschew is cooler and quieter: a standing habit of avoidance kept on principle, with no drama at all. You spurn one offer loudly; you eschew a practice for a lifetime.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

embrace: take something up eagerly

indulge: give in to something freely and with pleasure

Where it sits · how deliberate and cold the refusal

avoid → eschew → shun

avoid vs. eschew: Avoid is milder — you might avoid the highway at rush hour with no principle behind it at all; to eschew something is to rule it out always, on principle.

shun vs. eschew: Shun goes further than eschew: it adds cold contempt, usually aims at a person, and refuses all contact.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — eschew: to shy away from (Old French eschiver, from a Germanic word for dread)

Put it together: Eschew resists dissection — there is nothing to peel off here. It came into English whole from Old French eschiver, 'to shy away from,' which the Normans had themselves borrowed from a Germanic word for dread. The es- looks like a prefix but is not one English ever used, and no other common English word keeps the root.

Why there's no relative to spot: Eschew is a whole-word borrowing: Old French eschiver came from the same old Germanic family that gave us shy, but the connection wore invisible centuries ago, and no modern English word shares a recognizable piece of it. The word survives alone — a formal, slightly old-fashioned way to say you have sworn something off.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / bookish

Eschew is formal and bookish, best for named practices and things — a chef eschews shortcuts, a writer eschews jargon. It is a quiet standing policy, not a one-time act: abjure, taught in this unit, renounces something once, formally and in public, while shun turns cold contempt on a person. For everyday talk, plain 'avoid' or 'steer clear of' is the natural choice.
